title: Ukraine's ousted defense minister rejects Zelenskyy's offer of a different government role
description: Ukraine’s fired defense minister said Thursday he has rejected President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s efforts to persuade him to rejoin the government in a different role where he could continue fighting Rus...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine's fired defense minister said Thursday he has rejected President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's efforts to persuade him to rejoin the government in a different role where he could continue fighting Russia's more than 4-year-old invasion.

Mykhailo Fedorov, who was dismissed last week after just six months in the job, is a youthful and popular public figure due to his success in modernizing the armed forces and giving Ukraine an edge in the war through innovative use of technology. He has also cracked down on corruption in military procurement.

His departure triggered street protests across Ukraine that have put pressure on Zelenskyy and cheered Moscow officials.

Fedorov said in a statement that leading the Defense Ministry was one of only three jobs that "actually shape the course of the war," along with the presidency and chief of the armed forces.

He said that he would "not accept any position other than" defense minister, in what amounted to a defiant stance against Zelenskyy.

The Ukrainian president said earlier Thursday he had offered Fedorov the position of deputy prime minister for military innovation.

Fedorov said he wanted to finish his reforms at the Defense Ministry, which were cut short after his relationship soured with Soviet-trained commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who was viewed as part of the military old guard.

"No other role carries the actual authority to combat procurement corruption, complete the army's transformation, plan and execute asymmetric operations against the enemy, root out a culture of lies and unaccountability within the system," he said of the Defense Ministry post.

He said he took over last January with a plan to end the war by improving air defenses and holding firm on the front line while hurting Russia's economy through long-range strikes.

"Our collective results created something unprecedented, a window of opportunity to force Russia into peace through strength. And we cannot afford to lose it," he said.

title: Top US general says Ukraine's F-16s recently shot down their first Russian fighter jet, showing how far its air defense has come
description: Gen. Dan Caine said Ukraine scored its "first air-to-air kill where a Ukrainian F-16 shot down a Russian fighter," a mark of its progress.
fullText:
A top US general said a Ukrainian F-16 scored the country's first air-to-air kill.

He said it showed how far Ukraine's layered defenses have developed.

The general did not specify what kind of Russian fighter jet was shot down in the engagement.

Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets scored their first air-to-air kill by shooting down a Russian fighter jet, a top US general said, calling the engagement a sign of Ukraine's improving air defenses.

US Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said during a congressional hearing on Tuesday that "recently we had the first air-to-air kill where a Ukrainian F-16 shot down a Russian fighter."

He described it as evidence of Ukraine's growing air-defense capability.

"I think their ability to scale their layered defense has come a long way over the last couple years with the help and assistance of many," he said at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing.

An effective layered defense employs different sensors and weapons, positioned at varying distances and altitudes, to counter varied threats. It requires not only having enough sensors and weapons fielded, but also the ability to connect them, share information, and assign the right weapon to each threat.

Ukraine has expanded those defenses during Russia's full-scale invasion, combining domestically developed technology and Western weapons with Soviet-era systems already in service.

Caine did not provide details about the engagement, including where it occurred or what type of Russian aircraft was shot down. Some observers have speculated that he may have been referring to a July 8 Ukrainian Air Force claim that its forces downed a Russian Su-35. That, however, remains unclear.

The general cited the growth of Ukraine's defense industry and said he wanted to "highlight the incredible work that the Ukraine industrial base is doing as they scale their own capabilities. It ranges from their surface-to-air capabilities to their air-to-air capabilities." He was speaking in response to a question about what impact a potential US halting of air defense funding to Ukraine for three years would have.

Though it has significantly improved its defenses since the start of the war, including through domestic developments such as interceptor drones, Ukraine continues to ask for any and all air defense support it can get as Russian drone and missile bombardments worsen and continue to threaten both military and civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine received its first batch of F-16s in summer 2024 after a long debate among Western militaries about whether the provision of these fighter jets could be perceived as unnecessarily escalatory and how quickly Ukraine could integrate them and build the training, maintenance, logistics, and operational systems needed to use them effectively.

Ukraine has managed to integrate these assets into its air force, using them to intercept Russian drones and missiles, conduct strikes on ground targets, and now engage hostile crewed aircraft.

And Western partner nations are now studying how Ukraine combines cheap sensors, interceptor drones, dispersed operations, and older flying techniques to strengthen its air defenses and operations.

Partner nations are providing other advanced Western jets to Ukraine, including Swedish Gripens and French Mirages, framing it as both the result of Ukraine's competency and allied desire to integrate Ukraine into the future of Western defense, not just to have it survive this war.

President ‌Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on ⁠Tuesday that a young major general, Mykhailo Drapatyi, would replace Syrskyi after days of ⁠street protests.

The move followed the ousting in a wider government reshuffle last week of tech-savvy reformist defence minister ​Mykhailo Fedorov, ​which brought out into ​the open the deep ‌divisions in the Ukrainian defence leadership.

Syrskyi has held the commander in chief position since early 2024, after playing key roles in Kyiv's defence in the early days of the war and in a lightning counteroffensive ‌to retake swathes of the ​northeastern Kharkiv region in 2022.

But he ​has faced harsh ​criticism for a rigid command style which ‌some service members have said ​resulted in ​unjustifiably high troop losses.

title: Ukraine's arms makers say they need to figure out how to constantly update their weapons — without slowing output
description: Weapons makers must keep updating their gear before it's obsolete, but they have to do it without sacrificing the mass production modern wars demand.
fullText:
Ukraine's arms makers must constantly update weapons to keep them relevant.

But frequent redesigns can slow production when the military needs weapons at scale.

Companies are changing how they build gear to balance speed, scale, and adaptation.

Defense companies supplying Ukraine's army are trying to strike the right balance between constantly updating their weapons to stay on the cutting-edge of combat technology and producing enough of them for the fight against Russia's invasion.

The war is changing so quickly that battlefield technology can become outdated within weeks, forcing arms makers to continually adapt their products to new threats and countermeasures.

Companies have changed how they design and manufacture weapons to move faster. That said, arms makers still need to produce weaponry at scale for a war chewing through equipment at a rate rarely seen in recent Western conflicts.

Achi, the CEO of the Ukrainian-Estonian robot, drone, and software company Ark Robotics, told Business Insider that when "talking about scale manufacturing, any change comes at a very high price." Redesigning or making major changes can halt or slow production for long stretches and consume a lot of resources.

However, change is vital. "You cannot afford not to be able to make changes."

"We need our company to work at scale," Achi said. That means trying to chart the general trend of what's needed and what's going to be needed without taking too many risks or repeatedly disrupting production.

Striking the right balance, he said, is "really difficult.

The company takes risks at times to predict battlefield developments and shifts in the war, such as the bet it made at the beginning of last year that drone video and control links would shift from being mostly analog to increasingly being handled by onboard computers.

"That's kind of the big bet we made, and the engineering direction to make it possible," Achi said.

"We also don't want to get trapped too much in this constant change cycle. So we try to find the trend and stick to it because then we can deliver on mass and quality," he said.

With any of the changes it tests, the company always has to ask, "What could be the potential impact if we scaled it a thousand times?" Achi said.

"This iteration cycle is insane," he added. "I've never seen anything like it."

Gediminas Guoba, the CEO of Lithuanian drone maker Granta Autonomy, which has products in Ukraine, told Business Insider that trying to maintain that balance between producing at scale and making products that are well-suited to the requirements of the battlefield is crucial.

title: Ukraine's elite special operators are doing more infiltration missions as the front-line kill zone grows
description: Infiltration missions consist of small groups of soldiers who sneak past enemy lines to carry out raids or assault operations.
fullText:
Ukraine's elite soldiers have increased the number of infiltration missions they have conducted over the past year.

The uptick in missions comes as the drone-infested kill zone around the front line grows larger.

A Ukrainian special operator attributed this trend to a rise in Russian drones over the battlefield.

Elite Ukrainian special operators are carrying out more infiltration missions into Russian-held territory as the drone-infested kill zone continues to grow, making larger maneuvers difficult.

Infiltration operations typically involve small groups of soldiers sneaking past enemy lines to complete a mission, which can range from taking a key position to conducting ambushes, raids, and assaults.

For Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, "the number of missions has increased over the past year," an operator in the 4th Ranger Regiment told Business Insider in a recent interview.

The expansion of the kill zone has the Ukrainians not only executing more infiltration-style missions but also tasking operators to confront the challenges posed by similar Russian activities.

The 4th Ranger Regiment operator, who is the second-in-command of a small unit and requested to be identified only by his call sign "Gur" for security reasons, said he tends to receive "specific, targeted missions."

"We might be tasked with destroying one particular enemy position. We go in, destroy it, and come back out," Gur said, per a translation of his remarks. "That might take two days, four days, or a week. We don't necessarily have to stay in the area for a fixed amount of time."

To manage the increased tempo, Ukrainian special operators will rotate teams for these missions, allowing soldiers to rest, train, and prepare.

Ukrainian soldiers and officials often describe the front line as a "kill zone," an area heavily saturated with drones that can quickly attack troops and military vehicles, making any movement very dangerous. Drones are responsible for roughly 90% of all battlefield strikes.

The kill zone varies in width across the battlefield, though it typically extends roughly 10 to 20 kilometers in either direction from the line of contact. However, Ukrainian soldiers and officials have said it is expanding, forcing commanders to make tactical adjustments.

Gur attributed the expanding kill zone to the further proliferation of first-person-view (FPV) drones — cheap quadcopters rigged with explosives to deliver precision strikes. Ukrainian infiltration missions have increased concurrently with similar Russian operations.

"They're using our tactics as well," the operator said. "They infiltrate in groups of two to four soldiers, and they can make their way into our rear areas. Then that becomes another task for us. We have to go in and eliminate them."

Ukrainian soldiers said last year that Russian infiltration had become increasingly problematic during the war. The missions varied; some focused on holding positions, while others targeted key defenses. But they were largely designed to distract and cause chaos.

A senior Ukrainian defense official told Business Insider in late 2025 that small Russian infiltration teams were exploiting bad weather to sneak into Ukrainian-held territory and sow trouble. These missions are high-risk and can be deadly for those involved.

Front-line Ukrainian units don't always have the numbers to effectively cover all the territory they hold, Gur said. So when the Russians infiltrate, his group may get assigned to handle the breach.

"Basically," he said, "the Russians are our task."

The expanding kill zone has also pushed Ukrainian special operators to start using ground robots for logistics closer to the front lines and to evacuate casualties, both of which have become too dangerous for soldiers with the current drone presence.

"War creates its own conditions. FPV drones appeared, so we have to react to that," Gur said. "We have to adapt somehow if we want to survive and keep operating."

title: Ukraine's weapons makers fear a costly slowdown after their tech champion was pushed out of the defense ministry
description: Defense industry sources worry about what Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal could mean for battlefield innovation at a pivotal moment in the war.
fullText:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's reformist defense minister, last week.

The move has caused unease among Ukrainian manufacturers, who praised Fedorov's innovative approach.

Industry sources said they are concerned about the potential impact on Ukraine's war efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's surprise dismissal of his reformist defense minister has sent shockwaves through the country, causing unease and anxiety as Kyiv enjoyed a wave of fresh momentum on the battlefield.

Ukrainian defense industry sources described the removal of 35-year-old Mykhailo Fedorov last week, after just six months on the job, as a major disappointment for the country's powerhouse military-technology sector, expressing concerns about serious problems down the road.

A Ukrainian defense tech company representative who asked only to be identified as Anton said that Fedorov "was driving innovations, visionary goals, and very brave practical operations that gave President Zelenskyy his cards."

Anton said that Fedorov was proactive rather than reactive in his efforts to substantially overhaul Ukrainian weapons development, tactics, and doctrine, adding that "he was fulfilling today's needs and gaps while building tomorrow's relevance and superiority to ensure our victory."

Fedorov, who previously served as Ukraine's minister for digital transformation and is known for his Silicon Valley-style approach to the war, was appointed by Zelenskyy in January to oversee the defense ministry.

He quickly pushed to dramatically reform Ukraine's military, including placing greater emphasis on deploying drones and reshaping the contracting system. Fedorov also sought to overhaul the defense industry to increase development and make the procurement process more transparent and efficient.

Russia's invasion has turned Ukraine into a central hub for robotics and drone innovation. Hundreds of companies are building new technologies — from drones to electronic warfare devices — for the military, and many have their eyes set on future exports.

During Fedorov's tenure, Ukrainian firms enjoyed a much more transparent procurement process with the government, Anton said. He described collaborating with the defense ministry as a "professional and very productive" dialogue, "something we never could imagine before."

He said that Fedorov transformed the defense industry to meet the challenges of a changing battlefield, one that is becoming increasingly autonomous.

Since January, Ukrainian forces have been significantly ramping up their long-range drone strikes on Russian oil facilities and have used mid-range drones to hammer Russian logistics in the rear. The two campaigns have given Kyiv a sense of optimism and stymied Moscow's battlefield momentum while fueling its own.

Defense manufacturers see Ukraine's victories over the past few months as a testament to the drone-forward approach of Fedorov and his team.

The CEO of robotic systems maker Ark Robotics said that "policies supporting rapid deployment, streamlined procurement, and continuous battlefield feedback created the conditions for rapid technological progress."

Fedorov's emphasis on rapid technological change and decentralized innovation sometimes clashed with the military's more conventional command structure under Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi. Zelenskyy said the rift between the two had become a problem.

Zelenskyy omitted Fedorov from his government in a major reshuffle last week. The former defense minister said he was pushed out, and while he declined a government advisory role, it's unclear whether he could stay on in another capacity.

The dismissal caused confusion and anger among Ukrainian civilians and soldiers, and has stoked anxiety within the defense industry over the future of procurement and manufacturing priorities.

As defense minister, "Fedorov built a system where only equipment that actually worked and delivered results made it to the front," a Ukrainian manufacturer said, adding that "he created a competitive environment: manufacturers competed on quality, lowered their prices, and still met the front's real needs."

They said they worry about a potential backslide to "manual, top-down control."

Another Ukrainian manufacturer said they are "deeply concerned" as a producer, not only because of Fedorov's dismissal but also because Kyiv has gone through three defense ministers in a little over a year.

"This creates an unpredictable frame for work," they said. "Changing a minister and his team usually takes time to adjust all processes. This means that the adoption of necessary decisions can be slower for some time. Thus, this can affect our work as well."

Zelenskyy said that he asked Maj. Gen. Yevhen Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's SBU internal security agency, to lead the defense ministry in the interim.

Khmara previously led the SBU's elite Alpha unit, which has been the tip of the spear for Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia, so drone innovation may remain a priority for the defense ministry.

The Ark Robotics CEO said it remains to be seen whether Ukraine has the "institutional, strategic commitment to realize the same vision going forward and accelerate the changes" that Fedorov started.

Proper policies will enable defense innovation to move at the rapid pace required in a modern war, they said. "Our take is that being radical in implementing widespread use of unmanned systems is an existential question for Ukraine."

Without Fedorov at the helm, Ukrainian defense manufacturers don't see their efforts completely collapsing. However, they are worried about a potential change in pace that could prove harmful at a pivotal moment in the war.

"What happens to the industry, army, and country without Minister Fedorov?" Anton said. "Heaven will not fall on earth; the industry will work, as we all have a strong motivation to win this war, or at least not to lose."

"We will continue doing our best, as well as the guys in the trenches," he said, but there's a risk that "we will lose the pace of development."

title: Ukraine unleashes more than 400 drones near Moscow in one of war's biggest attacks
description: More than 400 drones targeted Moscow in one of Ukraine's largest attacks, striking an oil depot and logistics facilities more than 250 miles from the border.
fullText:
Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks of the war against Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, striking an oil depot and logistics facilities more than 250 miles from the Ukrainian border, according to Ukrainian and Russian officials.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said more than 400 Ukrainian drones were launched toward the Moscow region between Sunday evening and early Monday, including 85 that were destroyed while approaching the Russian capital. Russia's Defense Ministry separately claimed that its forces intercepted 381 drones across Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

The Russian claims could not be independently verified by Fox News Digital.

At least 10 people were wounded in the Moscow region, including three Chinese nationals, according to regional authorities cited by Reuters. Seven of the injuries were reported in Domodedovo, Russia, where officials said a residential building was struck and a fire broke out at an industrial park near one of Moscow's main airports.

The scale and reach of the operation suggest Ukraine is moving beyond occasional symbolic attacks on Moscow and building a sustained campaign against the infrastructure that supports Russia's war.

Ukraine Launches What Appears To Be One Of Its Largest Drone Attacks Against Russia: Report

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries had doubled since the beginning of 2026, Reuters reported, contributing to refinery shutdowns and reduced production of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian forces targeted logistics facilities and an oil depot in the Moscow region.

"Our long-range sanctions have produced results against logistics facilities and an oil depot," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that the targets were more than 400 kilometers (roughly 250 miles) from Ukraine's border. "We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities."

Wildberries, a company known as "Russia's Amazon," said its logistics center in the Podolsk district of Russia was temporarily evacuated as a precaution before resuming normal operations, East2West News reported. Ukraine has accused the company of selling supplies used by the Russian military.

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

Ksenia Svetlova, associate fellow at Chatham House policy institute based in London, argued that the disruption caused by strikes on fuel infrastructure and companies such as Wildberries is unlikely, by itself, to change President Vladimir Putin's approach to the war.

"The hardship of the Russian citizen who suffers because of fuel shortages, the strike on a Wildberries warehouse, or forced recruitment does not interest him," Svetlova said. "The war machine is operating at full force, and he has neither the desire nor the ability to stop it."

Svetlova said Putin remains reluctant to announce another mass mobilization after large numbers of young Russians fled the country during the Kremlin's previous call-up. At the same time, she said, Russia's military still needs additional troops after recruiting heavily from its prison population and is increasingly pressuring ordinary civilians accused of relatively minor offenses to sign military contracts.

The sweeping Ukrainian operation followed one of Russia's largest ballistic missile attacks of the war against Kyiv. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 41 missiles of various types in the overnight barrage, which killed at least one person and wounded 16, Reuters reported Sunday.

The Russian attack also spread into the Black Sea, where a Russian missile attack on the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Golden Leo killed 10 people near Odesa, Reuters reported Monday.

'A New Kind Of War': Inside Ukraine's Hidden Factories Mass-producing Combat Drones

Ukrainian officials said the vessel, which was carrying corn, was struck by three cruise missiles and caught fire. Nine crew members and a Ukrainian maritime pilot were killed, while eight other crew members were rescued. The ship's crew included Indian and Syrian nationals, according to Reuters.

The escalation comes as Zelenskyy faces growing domestic pressure over his removal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, a 35-year-old reformer credited with expanding Ukraine's drone capabilities and seeking to modernize military procurement and management. Fedorov's supporters viewed him as a rare official willing to challenge entrenched practices, improve oversight of defense spending and push a technology-centered approach to the war.

Thousands of demonstrators gathered following Fedorov's dismissal, demanding his reinstatement and the removal of commander-in-chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi. Protesters have accused Syrskyi of resisting modernization and retaining a rigid command structure that they say contributes to high troop losses. Syrskyi has defended his wartime record and called for unity.

Fedorov publicly accused Syrskyi of blocking his initiatives and sabotaging his work. Zelenskyy said their relationship had deteriorated so badly that the two could no longer work together, but provided little additional explanation for removing Fedorov.

Zelenskyy indicated Monday that consultations over Ukraine's military leadership were continuing, saying he had spoken with Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi about ensuring that the experience of every branch of Ukraine's defense forces was applied in a coordinated manner. He did not announce any decision on Syrskyi's future.

title: ‘Everyone's afraid to die’: Struggle to recruit soldiers in Ukraine turns violent
description: Aggression against recruitment officers has become increasingly threatening, police say.
fullText:
Vasyl Krupych knows what it is to fight for Ukraine.

He describes terrifying scenes from battles in the eastern Donbas region where, sometimes praying, sometimes crying, the machine gunner somehow survived the onslaught by Russian troops.

But last December, by then serving in the rear, Krupych was attacked by his own countrymen whilst out searching for draft dodgers.

He says two men ignored demands to show their documents and fled. When his patrol gave chase, Krupych was badly beaten with a crowbar. He spent six weeks in hospital.

"He broke my rib, I was lying there and couldn't breathe," the veteran recalled in a recent interview.

"What did we fight for, if soldiers can now get beaten?"

Ukraine's military ombudswoman says such attacks are now "regular" and "a major problem" as the country struggles to mobilise men to fight in the fifth, draining year of Russia's full-scale invasion.

It's not a topic people here care to discuss much, wary of feeding Russian propaganda.

But the latest National Police Service report recorded more than 600 assaults on recruitment officers to date and warned that the aggression has become "increasingly threatening".

The first big alert came in April when several recruiters were stabbed, one fatally. Then this month in Lviv, some 200 protesters surrounded officers attempting to detain a suspected draft dodger and smashed and overturned their car.

The riot made headlines as President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned violence against serving soldiers.

His controversial decision since then to sack Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov – over a clash of character and vision with Ukraine's commander-in-chief – means attempts to address the conscription crisis will stall.

But the anger that just exploded in Lviv suggests that the need is urgent.

The reasons appear to range from plain fear of the front line – now everyone knows someone who's been injured or killed - to a reluctance to 

The only surge of enthusiasm since the initial rush to the front was in late 2023, when Ukraine launched a counter-offensive to seize back territory in the south-east.

That's when the "brutal mobilisation" phase began, according to opposition MP Oleksandr Honcharenko.

He blames that for the backlash.

"These officers are hunting for people on the streets and sometimes using quite violent methods," the MP says.

"Violence leads to violence. It's a huge problem and it's going to get worse."

Military analyst Ivan Stupak agrees.

"We started to suffer a lack of manpower on the battlefield, constant losses," he recalls. "Ukraine's high command had to refill these losses so they started busification."

That's the term Ukrainians use for mobile patrols that end up with men bundled into buses, and off to serve.

"When they need an extra 5,000 men, they start grabbing them - and if they refuse it turns into fights on the street."

So for every story of a draft officer attacked, there are accounts of violence by recruiters themselves.

Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner recorded more than 6,000 such complaints last year - double the 2024 tally. They include claims of abuse and unlawful detention as well as poor conditions at recruitment centres.

Kyrylo Ogdansky still gets upset when he talks about what happened to him in Dnipro last November.

The university professor, who is exempt from the draft, was approached in the street by a man in plain clothes who wanted to check his call-up status.

There are rules about such patrols, including having police officers present, so Ogdansky objected.

"One of them knocked the phone from my hand and two pushed me into the bus from behind. When I asked what's happening, one started to beat me to the head. He hit me in the nose several times," Ogdansky tells me.

He remembers the threat to send him straight to the front line. "He said 'I can call the commander and you'll go to Pokrovsk'."

Instead, the professor spent two weeks in hospital with a suspected neck injury and big purple-black bruises beneath his eyes.

He has made formal official complaints but was hesitant about speaking publicly, aware that such things look bad for Ukraine in the middle of a war.

"Russian propaganda uses such things very actively. But such a problem exists," Ogdansky explains his decision.

"If everyone is silent, then why would it stop? I understand the problem of conscription, but no official has the right to act like this."

It's clear that Vasyl Krupych experienced horrors at war.

He volunteered at the very start and has survived some of the grimmest battles.

Krupych is proud of his service - a tattoo on his neck declares "Glory to the Ukrainian Armed Forces" – but he suffers from nightmares.

When his vehicle was hit by an FPV drone, he was badly injured but managed to drag one friend to safety. He saw two others burned to death.

Now, when we discuss the increase in attacks against draft officers, his words drip with hurt.

It's not just about what he suffered himself: that case is still going through the courts. It's also the gulf between what he has endured and those doing everything possible to avoid the same.

"We are doing our duty. We fought, we defended our people - and now they are attacking us."

I wonder what he thinks might motivate people to serve, instead of coercing them, and he mentions raising salaries.

"It can't be done differently, it can't. Our lads need to be replaced. But nobody volunteers," he says.

In his six months as defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov did start introducing reforms to tackle the growing crisis.

He began with moves meant to make military service more attractive: fixed-term contracts for new recruits, with the option to defer further service, and better salaries, especially for the riskiest roles.

But it was an early work in progress and overhauling conscription was still on his to-do list when he was sacked.

Proposals have included handing draft patrols over to police, who are less personally invested in the task. There's talk of proper training, too, for officers, and psychological screening.

Ukraine does admit openly that it has a problem, which is new.

But it now has only an acting defence minister, and still no solution.

title: Russian online retail warehouses hit by deadly Ukrainian strikes
description: Drones targeted Wildberries facilities near Moscow and in Tambov. Ukraine's leader called them "major logistics facilities" supplying "sanctioned components".
fullText:
Watch: Huge warehouse blaze in Moscow region following Ukrainian strikes

Eight people have been killed and 62 injured after Ukrainian drones struck two warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, according to Russian officials.

Seven deaths and 25 injuries occurred at a warehouse in the city of Tambov, roughly 295 miles (475km) south-east of Moscow. One death and 37 injuries occurred at another Wildberries warehouse in Elektrostal in the Moscow region.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks had struck "major logistics facilities" which had been used to "supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment".

He added that Ukraine had also struck targets in the Sea of Azov, the Black Sea, and Russian-annexed Crimea.

The attacks appear to have started at night, with some videos showing terrified and injured staff attempting to flee as explosions continue. Another clip appears to show the walls of a warehouse disintegrating as they are engulfed by flames.

Zelensky said Ukraine's operations were in response to "Russian strikes on our civilian infrastructure and on our cities and communities". Overnight into Wednesday, 14 people were killed in Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Wildberries is often described as the Russian equivalent of Amazon. The merged RWB group, which combines Wildberries with advertising company Russ, was valued at about $12.6bn (£9.3bn) by Forbes Russia in 2026.

Serhii Kuzan, chairman of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre, told the BBC that Wildberries was a "vital component" of Russian logistics, and that its website had been used by Russian volunteers to purchase military equipment including walkie-talkies, body armour and drone components.

"The primary rationale for striking Wildberries' warehouses is to disrupt Russian logistics and the supply of dual-use goods, critical electronics, sanctioned goods and the like to the Russian army and Russian arms manufacturers," he said.

"The collateral damage from such strikes could also have a serious impact on the Russian economy, as well as a psychological effect on Russian society and, likely, on continued support for the war."

Russia has targeted similar facilities in Ukraine since the start of the war, including its postal service and some electronics distributors.

Wildberries ​CEO ​Tatyana Kim - one of Russia's first female billionaires - ⁠said it had been a "terrible night" for Russia and for the company.

"Seven people working the night shift died on the spot," governor of the Tambov region Evgeniy Pervyshov wrote on Telegram, adding that 28 drones were also shot down on approach.

He said 25 people had been injured, including seven in serious condition. Most of these injuries were caused by shrapnel wounds, he said.

It was the "largest and most inhumane" attack on the region in terms of the number of drones used and the number of casualties, he added.

Meanwhile, governor of the Moscow region Andrei Vorobyov said eight of those injured in the strikes on the Wildberries warehouse in Elektrostal were in a "serious condition".

He added that a total of 48 drones were shot down in the region overnight, and that a Russian oil depot had also been struck by a falling drone, which he described as the incident with "the most serious consequences".

"Firefighters, emergency services, and the Ministry of Emergency Situations continue to work at the scene," he wrote on Telegram. He did not describe the level of damage in detail. Zelensky separately confirmed Ukraine had struck "an oil facility".

Ukraine has recently intensified its long-range drone attacks on Russia's critical energy infrastructure, causing widespread fuel shortages. Earlier this month, Kyiv said nearly 43% of Russia's oil refining capacity had been "disabled" as a result.

The BBC has not independently verified this figure.

Ukraine says Russian oil and gas facilities are legitimate targets as Moscow relies heavily on fossil fuel exports to finance its full-scale invasion, which began in February 2022.

Russian President Vladimir Putin made a rare admission in June that fuel shortages had been caused by Ukrainian attacks, and signed into law a bill aimed at boosting supplies to the domestic fuel market in early July.
